citation.author: Wright, Esther
citation.title: Rockstar Games, Red Dead Redemption, and Narratives of 'Progress'
citation.venue: European Journal of American Studies 16-3 (Special Issue: Video Games and/in American Studies); DOI 10.4000/ejas.17300

discipline: American Studies; game history; historical game studies; industry & paratext studies
thesis: Rockstar deploys narratives of 'progress' across three levels-developer-brand image, the franchise's promotional surround, and in-game text-and this is self-contradictory: the Frontier-mythic civilization/savagery discourse used to brand and sell the games is precisely what the games claim to critique, leaving the critique selective, surface-level, and undercut by Rockstar's reliance on (and profit from) the ideologies of progress, white supremacy, settler colonialism, and capitalist 'civilization' it gestures at condemning.
sections: Introduction (PC re-release as 'progress'; three-level argument; irony as 'no-lose gambit')
The Rockstar Brand and Open-World Development (Outlaws for Life; problem-child vs industry-leader; Rockstar World; digi-Whiggish game history)
The 'True West' and an 'Evolving' America (paratextual authenticity network; developer-historian; faux-historical ads; homesteader myth; labor-irony)
'It's reverse Integration...or regressive acculturation...'; or, 'Eugenics for Beginners' (Reservations; Nastas/MacDougal; race science; Saint Denis eugenics encounter; false equivalence)
Conclusion: The Outlaw Brand's 'Frontier' Narrative(s) (progress as moral-disengagement device; muddled politics; branding undermines critique)
concepts: narratives of 'progress' (historical content + marketing rhetoric + brand self-description)
authenticity as constructed/marketed discourse (not accuracy, not feel)
irony as 'no-lose gambit' / 'have your cake and eat it too' / self-cancellation
digi-Whiggish / teleological game historiography (Murray, Nooney, Therrien)
the 'safety valve' / yeoman-homesteader myth vs historical reality
racism without racists / 'I don't see color' (Blake)
readings: Both games structure narrative AND gameplay around a lament for the passing age of outlaws and loss of free Western space for white male outlaws.

Domestic/'chores' gameplay dramatizes the lost homesteader ideal but ends 'always unavoidably tragic,' denying the ideal Western life; read against the ~10% individual-homesteader statistic (Trachtenberg/Shannon).
The critique of 'civilization' is a superficial repurposing of revisionist-Western themes (The Wild Bunch, Unforgiven); the politics 'read as hopelessly muddled.'
Native American characters function only as a device to position white outlaws as oppositional to 'the Law'; their value is 'directly proportional to their otherness.'
The franchise elicits greatest sympathy for white male protagonists as victims, not Indigenous peoples-a false equivalence confining genocide to 'the past.'

The Saint Denis eugenics encounter and MacDougal subplot reduce race science to 'idiotic' and 'of the past,' aligning the games with individual-bad-racist framing (Anderson) rather than structural critique (Saini).
Rockstar's brand narrative of industrial 'progress' (pushing development 'frontiers') mirrors and reinforces the historical 'progress' narrative inside the games.

game_elements.element: RDR2 PC announcement/launch trailer (Arthur Morgan voiceover: 'more and more civilization, what a damn mess we're making of things')
game_elements.how_treated: Used as epigraph and recurring anchor; example of how progress/civilization discourse pervades the promotional surround and frames player expectation.

game_elements.element: 'The True West - History That Helped Inspire Red Dead Redemption' Newswire blog series (Frank James; Western Weaponry; New Inventions; Patent Medicines, Drink and Drugs; The Brands of RDR)
game_elements.how_treated: Read as positioning Rockstar in pedagogical 'developer-historian' role, commodifying research and constructing 'a discourse of historical authenticity'; historicizes the turn-of-century world via progress/transition/modernization.

game_elements.element: Faux-historical in-game advertisements / Wheeler & Rawson Co. mail-order catalogue (Cattleman Revolver advert)
game_elements.how_treated: The purchasing interface for provisions/weapons/clothing; the revolver ad's labor copy ('skilled laborers...little pay') exposes irony against Rockstar's own 'crunch' culture (Schreier); 'have their cake and eat it too.'

Historically contextualizes 1899 'evolving' America; 'civilization spreading rapidly into the huge, wild and lawless frontier'; frames the game as capturing the 'pivotal moment when the age of outlaws was ending.'

game_elements.element: Cochinay Reservation, RDR (missions 'And You Will Know the Truth' / 'And the Truth Will Set You Free')
game_elements.how_treated: Inaccessible except in third-act missions where Marston storms it with the US Army; 'wiping out every last man' is a predetermined objective-a micro-scale recreation of genocidal violence; Marston implicated despite no overt racism.

game_elements.element: Wapiti Reservation, RDR2 (Eagle Flies dialogue, mission 'Favored Sons')
game_elements.how_treated: Populated by 'the old and infirm'; young 'shipped off to reform schools'; reinforces 'vanishing American' trope (Dippie); aligns Native threatened-extinction with white outlaws' extinction (false equivalence).

game_elements.element: Harold MacDougal & Nastas, RDR (mission 'At Home with Dutch')
game_elements.how_treated: Disgraced Yale professor performing race science ('reverse Integration'/'regressive acculturation'); played off rational Nastas; 'played for laughs'; despite 'obvious distaste' (Margini), centering of Marston makes it hard to read as meaningful critique.

game_elements.element: 'Eugenics for Beginners' pamphlet / Professor Norris Forsythe NPC encounter, RDR2
game_elements.how_treated: Arthur's 'I've known good, bad, and dumb white people' / 'I don't see color' pre-scripted response (Blake on racism-without-racists); satchel description 'a racist, idiotic eugenics handbill'; reduces eugenics to 'idiotic' and 'of the past'; NPC dispensed of for calling Arthur 'dumb,' not for racism.

'A representation of all that is wrong with American modernity and progress'; site of multiple satirical NPC encounters (eugenicist, suffragette, get-rich-quick proto-entrepreneur) given 'equivalent weighting'-another false and damaging equivalence.

game_elements.element: Law-and-order antagonists: Agent Ross (RDR), Agent Milton (RDR2), Colonel Favours; Milton/Dutch cutscene exchange
game_elements.how_treated: Stand-ins for US government policy; the Milton ('This is a civilized land now...') vs Dutch ('ain't no such thing as civilized...found only appetites') exchange is 'emblematic' of the games' critique-yet 'hardly a radical revision' (Keller).

game_elements.element: Red Dead Online roles (Bounty Hunter, Trader, Trapper)
game_elements.how_treated: Player 'becomes whatever kind of Westerner' satisfying the desire to exist in the virtual West; instances the colonial 'exploration and mastering of digital space' critique (Lammes; Mukherjee; Murray).

game_elements.element: Optional KKK rallies & 'The Iniquities of History' / Jeremiah Compson side mission (slave-catcher's ledger), RDR2
game_elements.how_treated: Cited (footnote) as further ambivalent inclusions that 'raise more questions than they answer' about whether such elements are valid critique/satire or box-checking.

themes: authenticity collapsing into ideology when paratext is read with text
doubling of 'progress' (industrial/brand progress mirrors historical/diegetic progress)
corporate 'have it both ways' irony in the games industry
settler colonialism and the Indian 'absent presence'
white male victimhood as the franchise's emotional center
race science/eugenics as comic anachronism vs living structure
labor, crunch, and the gap between depicted and actual exploitation

debate_axis_positions.position: Firmly critical; among the sharpest critics of Rockstar's self-presentation ('criticism that merely scratches the surface'), but a structural/ideological critic who declines to assign Rockstar 'full brunt of responsibility' (they 'capitalize on' a wider capitalist recycling of images).

Reframes the axis to authenticity-as-constructed/marketed-discourse; refuses to grade the games on accuracy yet turns that concession into a sharper question-why make authenticity claims at all if exempt from historical standards?
Distinctively insists text and paratext be read together; paratext casts a 'harsher light' on ideological resonance-the methodological axis she most pushes the field toward.

tensions: Concedes it may be 'unrealistic to expect a video game' to carry nuanced historiography, yet holds authenticity-claims forfeit that excuse.
Allows the games 'suggest an awareness' of representational stakes and that it would be 'overly simplistic' to say Rockstar are not critical-but awareness != sustained critique.
Acknowledges historical games' radical potential (Chapman) while arguing these titles default to a 'historiographic status quo' (Uricchio).

Brand 'progress' (innovation/development) and diegetic 'progress' (modernization/civilization) are framed as mutually reinforcing yet are also held in critical opposition as the source of the contradiction.
The labor-irony of the Cattleman Revolver ad is judged 'unlikely' to be self-reflexive even as it functions as the article's clearest instance of the contradiction.
